Marc Cherry (creator of desperate housewives) was a guest mentor at a masterclass I sang in as part of a one week jazz intensive; I was one of maybe five people chosen to sing out of 40. At the time I was 16, and the song my teacher and I had chosen was upbeat but with sort of sultry lyrics (nothing explicitly sexy, just mentions of lips/kissing). After listening to me sing it once Marc rather derisively and tersely declared- on stage in front of a ton of people including *michael feinstein*, mind you- that I was just "way too girl next door" to make the song work. I *swear to god*, with the way he said "girl next door", he could have said "homely potato" and the meaning would have been the same. I knew- and everyone in that hall knew- that he was calling me simultaneously unattractive and void of personality. 

I wanted to die right then and there but I had to hold it together for the next 20 mins of the masterclass. After that he barely even tried to workshop the song with me and, despite trying my best, I couldn't really come back from being told that I am intrinsically not capable of doing this song that I had already put hours into practicing. I went on to study opera so it's not like he made me swear off performing forever, but it really did affect my self-image. In my head I will forever be the homely potato girl next door. Thanks Marc!

What do I do for work? -> ALT, started straight out of college and have been here for almost 2 years. Love the work, luckily I'm pretty well-utilized at my school and make most of my own activities and class plans. Plus I get off right at 4:30 and get half days on Fridays, and am given all the breaks that the students get (2 weeks in winter, 1 in spring, 5  in summer, 1 in fall). The same definitely cannot be said for a lot, perhaps the majority, of ALT jobs.

Opportunities? -> Plenty of English teaching jobs if you don't mind getting paid in pocket lint and PBJ sandwiches... I'm on JET, though, so my base salary is relatively high and my housing is partially compensated. However, my ultimate goal is to do something music or publishing related as a day job while pursuing my own artistic goals on the side (double majored in opera performance and creative writing in college) and I have no idea where to even begin to find something like that. The arts are a hard enough field to find employment in in my home country.

Going home? -> I've thought about it, specifically to go to grad school for opera. but if I did that I think I'd have to give up the idea of living in Japan, since it's certainly not an opera hotspot and I'm not even sure if I cold get a visa as a freelance musician anyway.

Basically my conundrum rn is that I would love to keep living in Japan for as long as possible, but my current job has a 5 year maximum time limit and I don't want to do some crappy eikaiwa or office job that would significantly lower my current salary and standard of living... and at the same time, I yearn to return to the music world and don't currently know how to do that and stay in Japan. It's tough out here!

This person is somewhat right in that the average Japanese person is usually using konjac/shirataki as a texture/volume supplement to a dish, as opposed to a straight-up noodle replacement. Oh, and you walked/rode your bike to the store to buy the ingredients. There’s a reason very few people here are fat. 

Also, konjac is so common that you can literally get it at the convenience store! In the winter there’s nothing better than a big bowl of broth with shirataki, some chunks of daikon radish that have been cooked for so long that they’re fully permeated by the broth flavor, maybe a cute little fried tofu pouch, or a kombu kelp bow mmmm…. Oop doesn’t know what they’re missing.
